description: A cognitive distortion in which an individual predicts future outcomes — almost always negative — and treats those predictions as established facts rather than possibilities. Unlike productive planning or realistic risk assessment, fortune telling operates with false certainty, foreclosing openness to other outcomes and generating anticipatory anxiety, avoidance, and hopelessness disproportionate to actual probabilities.

templates.title: Predicting Failure Before Trying
templates.explanation: Fortune telling most commonly appears at the threshold of new efforts — job applications, difficult conversations, creative pursuits, or personal challenges — where the mind pre-emptively declares failure before any attempt has been made. This prediction is then used to justify avoidance, which prevents the very experience that could disconfirm the forecast. Over time, the pattern narrows life progressively as more and more domains are abandoned to predicted failure.
templates.reflection_question: How accurately have your negative predictions about outcomes actually tracked with what eventually happened? If you reviewed your last ten feared outcomes, how many materialized in the way — and to the degree — you predicted they would?
templates.balanced_reframe: A prediction is not a fact — it is a hypothesis about an uncertain future, generated by an anxious mind that specializes in threat detection rather than accurate forecasting. The outcome of an untried effort is genuinely unknown, and unknown is not the same as doomed. The only way to test the prediction is to act despite it.
templates.behavioral_action: Before your next avoided task, write the specific negative prediction down with a confidence rating (0–100%). After completing the task, return to what you wrote and compare the prediction to the actual outcome. Over time, this record becomes concrete evidence of your forecasting accuracy — or inaccuracy.

templates.title: Forecasting Rejection in Social Situations
templates.explanation: Social fortune telling involves predicting — with near certainty — that others will react with judgment, disinterest, mockery, or rejection before any interaction has taken place. This anticipatory certainty generates the same physiological and emotional response as actual rejection, priming avoidance behaviors that limit social connection and deprive the person of corrective experiences. The forecast, never tested, remains permanently unchallenged.
templates.reflection_question: In past social situations where you predicted rejection or judgment, how often did the interaction unfold exactly as you feared? What range of outcomes — including neutral and positive ones — have actually occurred when you engaged despite the prediction?
templates.balanced_reframe: Social outcomes are among the least predictable of all human experiences — shaped by the other person's mood, their own preoccupations, context, and countless variables outside your awareness or control. Treating your anxious forecast as the most reliable available information about how others will respond dramatically underestimates the genuine uncertainty — and possibility — of each interaction.
templates.behavioral_action: Identify one social situation you have been avoiding due to a negative prediction. Before engaging, write the specific predicted outcome. Afterward, record what actually happened. Pay particular attention to neutral outcomes — interactions that were simply unremarkable — as these are consistently underrepresented in anxious forecasting.

templates.title: Predicting That Things Will Never Improve
templates.explanation: Fortune telling applied to the future course of one's life or circumstances produces one of its most clinically significant manifestations: hopelessness. The belief that things will not — or cannot — get better is experienced not as a fear or a worry but as a known fact about the future. This pseudo-certainty about an inherently uncertain future is a core cognitive feature of depression and a significant risk factor that warrants careful clinical attention.
templates.reflection_question: Has there been any period in your past when circumstances felt permanent and unchangeable — and yet eventually shifted in ways you did not anticipate at the time? What does that tell you about your ability to accurately predict the long-term trajectory of your life from within a period of pain?
templates.balanced_reframe: The future is genuinely, fundamentally unknown — and that uncertainty cuts in every direction. Predicting that nothing will improve requires the same certainty about the future that predicting improvement would — and neither is available to us. What is reliably true is that circumstances, relationships, understanding, and inner resources change in ways that are rarely visible from the depths of a difficult period.
templates.behavioral_action: Write down one area of life you are currently forecasting as permanently stuck or hopeless. Then identify one small, concrete action — however modest — that represents movement in that area. Taking the action is not about guaranteeing improvement; it is about demonstrating to yourself that the future is still open and that you retain some agency within it.

templates.title: Anticipating the Worst in Health and Safety
templates.explanation: Fortune telling frequently targets physical health and personal safety, converting ambiguous symptoms, routine medical appointments, or ordinary life risks into predicted catastrophes. This pattern overlaps with health anxiety and generalized anxiety disorder, and produces chronic anticipatory dread that can be as functionally impairing as actual illness. The certainty attached to the negative health prediction is almost always disproportionate to the available evidence.
templates.reflection_question: Looking back at health or safety concerns you have predicted with high certainty in the past — how many resulted in the outcome you feared? What has been the base rate of your most feared health predictions actually coming true, and how does that compare to the certainty you felt at the time?
templates.balanced_reframe: Ambiguous physical symptoms and health uncertainty are genuinely uncomfortable — and the impulse to resolve that uncertainty through prediction is understandable. However, the mind under anxiety reliably predicts the most threatening possibility, not the most statistically likely one. Consulting a professional for genuine concerns is grounded and appropriate; treating the anxious prediction itself as a diagnosis is not.
templates.behavioral_action: When a health-related fortune-telling thought arises, practice the two-step response: first, acknowledge the anxiety without acting on the prediction ('I notice I am predicting something serious — this is anxiety, not diagnosis'); second, identify whether a specific, grounded action — such as scheduling a medical consultation — would address the concern proportionately.

templates.title: Predicting How Others Will React to Honest Communication
templates.explanation: Fortune telling acts as a powerful barrier to authentic communication, with individuals predicting — and accepting as certain — that expressing a need, setting a boundary, sharing a feeling, or raising a concern will result in conflict, abandonment, ridicule, or irreparable damage to the relationship. This prediction silences legitimate communication and gradually erodes both self-expression and relational authenticity, often producing the very disconnection the person fears.
templates.reflection_question: Has there been a time when you expressed something honest and vulnerable — despite fearing the reaction — and the outcome was more manageable, or even more connecting, than your prediction suggested? What does that experience tell you about the reliability of your forecasts in this area?
templates.balanced_reframe: Most people, in most relationships, respond to honest and respectful communication with more understanding and flexibility than fortune telling predicts. While some conversations are genuinely difficult and outcomes are never guaranteed, silencing authentic expression in order to avoid a predicted negative reaction trades a possible difficulty for a certain one — the ongoing cost of unexpressed needs and unspoken truths.
templates.behavioral_action: Identify one communication you have been withholding due to a predicted negative reaction. Before having the conversation, write down your specific prediction. Approach the conversation with care and respect, then record what actually happened. Notice in particular whether the predicted catastrophic reaction materialized — or whether reality offered more complexity and possibility than the forecast allowed.

templates.title: Using Past Pain to Guarantee Future Outcomes
templates.explanation: A particularly entrenched form of fortune telling involves using painful past experiences as irrefutable evidence for what will happen in the future — 'It went wrong before, so it will go wrong again.' While past experience is genuinely informative, it is not deterministic. This pattern conflates the understandable caution that comes from prior hurt with a certainty about future outcomes that the past cannot actually provide, foreclosing growth, new relationships, and new possibilities.
templates.reflection_question: Are you treating a past painful outcome as a guarantee of future outcomes — rather than as one data point among many? What factors were present in that past situation that may not be present now: different people, different circumstances, a different version of yourself with more experience and awareness?
templates.balanced_reframe: Past experience is a teacher, not a prophet. Learning from what has gone wrong is adaptive and wise; concluding that what went wrong will inevitably repeat is a step beyond what the evidence supports. You are not the same person who faced that earlier difficulty, the circumstances are not identical, and the future has not yet been written.
templates.behavioral_action: Draw a simple two-column comparison: on one side, list the factors from the past painful experience that contributed to its outcome. On the other, list the ways the current situation differs — different people, different knowledge, different context, different you. Use this comparison to soften the certainty of the prediction and restore a more honest sense of genuine uncertainty.

clinical_note: These templates are intended as psychoeducational tools to complement — not replace — individualized therapeutic care. Fortune telling is a transdiagnostic feature prominent in generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, depression, health anxiety, and PTSD. The hopelessness variant (Template 3) warrants careful monitoring in depressive presentations and should prompt assessment of suicidal ideation where clinically indicated. Behavioral experiments — systematically testing predictions against real outcomes — are among the most empirically supported interventions for fortune telling and are strongly recommended as a structured adjunct to cognitive restructuring. Clinicians should also consider whether fortune telling in a given client may be rooted in genuinely adverse past experiences, warranting a trauma-informed approach to prediction-challenging.
